shorts_extract.hook: September 13, 1848 in Cavendish, Vermont: railroad foreman Phineas Gage turns his head while tamping blasting powder, a spark ignites the hole, and a 3-foot-7-inch iron rod shoots through his left cheek and out the top of his skull—yet minutes later he sits upright in an ox cart talking.
shorts_extract.core_experiment: The iron rod tore through the judgment center behind his left eye (ventromedial prefrontal cortex) and severed about 11% of his left frontal white-matter wiring from the emotional alarm (amygdala), leaving his speech and walk intact while wrecking his social filter so friends said he was 'no longer Gage'.
shorts_extract.twist: Instead of staying a ruined drifter forever as textbooks claim, Gage later worked for years in Chile driving a six-horse stagecoach on steep mountain roads, where strict daily routine helped his spared brain networks relearn control.

chapters.title: 4:30 PM in the Cavendish Cut
beats: Set the scene in September 1848 along the Rutland and Burlington Railroad cut in Cavendish, Vermont.
Explain the three-step blasting routine: black powder, protective sand plug, and tamping with Gage's custom 3-foot-7-inch, 13.25-pound iron rod.
Show the distraction: Gage looks over his right shoulder toward his crew before sand is poured, sparks the granite, and the rod blasts upward through his left cheek and skull.
new_shots_needed: Close-up of the assistant pouring black powder and reaching for the sand pail too late
Wide shot of the smeared iron rod landing 20-25 yards behind the granite ledge

chapters.title: The Walk Up the Hotel Stairs
beats: Gage speaks within minutes of the blast and rides three-quarters of a mile sitting upright in an ox cart.
At Joseph Adams's hotel, he steps out of the cart, climbs the stairs, and greets Dr. Edward Williams and Dr. John Harlow.
Detail the autumn 1848 infection crisis—fungal sprouts, prepared coffin, and Harlow draining eight ounces of pus—until the skull opening closes in January 1849.
new_shots_needed: Candlelit hotel bedroom showing Dr. Harlow dressing the cranial wound and draining the abscess

chapters.title: 'No Longer Gage': The Lost Foreman Job
beats: In spring 1849 Gage returns to Cavendish carrying his tamping iron and asks for his old foreman job back.
Show his sudden profanity, abandoned plans, and impatience with restraint in the tavern and contractor office; his bosses refuse to rehire him.
Dive inside the skull to show why speech and movement survived while the judgment center behind the left eye was destroyed.
new_shots_needed: Side-by-side comparison of intact left Broca's/motor strips versus the shattered left orbitofrontal base

chapters.title: Three Generations of Skull Scans (1994, 2004, 2012)
beats: Follow Gage's exhumed skull and tamping iron to Harvard's Warren Anatomical Museum.
Compare Damasio's 1994 bilateral model against Ratiu's 2004 thin-slice CT of the real skull proving strictly left-sided damage.
Break down Van Horn's 2012 connectome study: 4% cortical gray matter lost, 11% white-matter cables cut between the emotional alarm (amygdala) and the judgment center.
new_shots_needed: Museum tabletop view of Bigelow's 1850 plaster life cast beside the hinged skull flap

chapters.title: The Chile Stagecoach Twist and Social Recovery
beats: Debunk the textbook myth of the permanent violent drifter using Malcolm Macmillan's historical detective work.
Follow Gage to Valparaiso and Santiago, Chile, where he cares for horses and drives a heavily laden six-horse stagecoach for nearly seven years.
Show the 1850 Wilgus daguerreotype portrait—once mistaken for a whaler with a harpoon—and explain how structured daily routines help injured frontal brains recover.
new_shots_needed: 1850 daguerreotype studio recreation showing Gage posing upright with his inscribed iron bar
